meta.blurb: In fair Verona, two families have hated each other for years. Then a boy and a girl from opposite houses fall in love at first sight. Shakespeare's most famous love story is retold here for learners, from the secret wedding to its heartbreaking end.
meta.bible: Romeo Montague: the young, romantic son of the Montagues; he loves Juliet and is banished from Verona. Juliet Capulet: the daughter of the Capulets, not yet fourteen, brave and quick-witted. Lord Capulet and Lady Capulet: Juliet's parents; hot-tempered and proud. Lord Montague and Lady Montague: Romeo's parents; Lady Montague dies of grief when Romeo is banished. The Nurse: Juliet's old, talkative nurse. Friar Laurence: a kind friar who marries the lovers and hopes to end the feud; he makes the sleeping potion. Friar John: a friar sent with the letter to Romeo, who is stopped by plague quarantine. Tybalt: Juliet's fierce cousin, who kills Mercutio and is killed by Romeo. Mercutio: Romeo's witty, loyal friend and a relative of the Prince; he dies fighting Tybalt. Benvolio: Romeo's cousin and friend, a peacemaker. Paris: a noble young man, a relative of the Prince, who wishes to marry Juliet. Prince Escalus: the ruler of Verona, who forbids fighting on pain of death. Balthasar: Romeo's servant, who brings him the false news. Sampson and Gregory: Capulet servants who start the first brawl. Rosaline: a girl Romeo loves before he meets Juliet. The apothecary: the poor man in Mantua who sells Romeo poison. Verona: the Italian city of the story. Mantua: the city where Romeo is sent in exile. Fixed facts: the families are the Montagues and the Capulets; Romeo and Juliet meet at a Capulet feast and marry in secret the next day with Friar Laurence; Romeo kills Tybalt after Mercutio's death and is banished; Juliet takes a sleeping potion to avoid marrying Paris; the letter to Romeo never arrives; Romeo takes poison at the tomb, and Juliet ends her own life; the families end their feud at last. The play is from around 1595 and was written by William Shakespeare. Voice and tone: passionate, poetic and tragic, told clearly and kindly; deaths are stated plainly with no gore.

beats.scene: A sunlit Italian city with two noble houses facing each other across a square
beats.summary: In the city of Verona, two noble families, the Montagues and the Capulets, are old enemies.

beats.scene: Servants of both families push and shout at each other in a market
beats.summary: Servants from the two families begin a fight in the street.

beats.scene: Benvolio holds his sword up between the servants, as fierce Tybalt strides in
beats.summary: Benvolio tries to stop the fight, but Tybalt joins in and makes it worse.

beats.scene: Prince Escalus stands above the angry crowd, his hand raised to demand silence
beats.summary: The Prince warns that anyone who fights in the streets will be put to death.

beats.scene: Romeo sits alone under a tree at dawn, sighing, while Benvolio looks worried
beats.summary: Romeo is miserable because the girl he loves, Rosaline, does not love him.

beats.scene: A well-dressed Paris speaks seriously with Lord Capulet in his house
beats.summary: Paris asks Lord Capulet if he can marry Juliet, and Capulet tells him to wait.

beats.scene: A servant squints at a long list of names while Romeo and Benvolio watch
beats.summary: A servant who cannot read asks Romeo for help, and he learns about the Capulet feast.

beats.scene: Romeo, Benvolio and Mercutio walk through the night in masks and capes
beats.summary: Romeo and his friends go to the feast in masks, and Mercutio jokes about dreams.

beats.scene: Romeo, his mask lifted, stares across a crowded ballroom at a girl in white
beats.summary: At the feast, Romeo sees Juliet and forgets Rosaline at once.

beats.scene: Tybalt grips his sword as old Lord Capulet holds him back at the party
beats.summary: Tybalt recognises Romeo's voice, but Lord Capulet will not let him fight.

beats.scene: Romeo and Juliet hold hands and kiss in a corner of the great hall
beats.summary: Romeo and Juliet kiss, and then learn that they belong to enemy families.

beats.scene: Juliet leans on a stone balcony above a moonlit garden while Romeo hides below
beats.summary: Romeo climbs into the Capulet garden, and Juliet comes to her balcony and speaks of her love.

beats.scene: Romeo steps out of the shadows and looks up at Juliet on the balcony
beats.summary: Romeo answers Juliet, and the two promise to love each other.

beats.scene: Juliet leans down from the balcony as the first light of dawn appears
beats.summary: Romeo and Juliet agree to marry, and Juliet promises to send a messenger.

beats.scene: Friar Laurence picks herbs in his garden at sunrise
beats.summary: Romeo tells Friar Laurence that he is in love, and the friar is amazed.

beats.scene: Friar Laurence smiles thoughtfully as Romeo holds his hands in thanks
beats.summary: Friar Laurence agrees to marry them, hoping that it will end the feud.

beats.scene: Mercutio and Benvolio laugh in the street as the Nurse arrives
beats.summary: Romeo tells the Nurse the plan for the secret wedding.

beats.scene: The Nurse sits and fans herself while Juliet waits with shining eyes
beats.summary: The Nurse teases Juliet before telling her the plan, and Juliet hurries to the friar.

beats.scene: Romeo and Juliet stand before Friar Laurence in his small stone cell
beats.summary: Romeo and Juliet are married secretly by Friar Laurence.

beats.scene: Tybalt strides through a sunny square and points his sword at Romeo
beats.summary: Tybalt challenges Romeo to a fight, but Romeo refuses because Tybalt is now his cousin.

beats.scene: Mercutio draws his sword and faces Tybalt in the middle of the street
beats.summary: Mercutio, angry at Romeo's calm answer, fights Tybalt in his friend's place.

beats.scene: Romeo kneels beside the fallen Mercutio in the street
beats.summary: Mercutio dies and curses both families.

beats.scene: Romeo draws his sword as Tybalt comes back, and they fight
beats.summary: Romeo kills Tybalt in anger, and then he realises what he has done.

beats.scene: The Prince, Capulets and Montagues stand in the street around Tybalt's body
beats.summary: Prince Escalus banishes Romeo from Verona, saying he will die if he stays.

beats.scene: Juliet stands at her window as the Nurse hurries in, weeping
beats.summary: Juliet hears that Romeo has killed Tybalt and is torn between love and grief.

beats.scene: Romeo lies on the stone floor of the friar's cell, weeping
beats.summary: Romeo despairs in Friar Laurence's cell, and the friar tells him to be strong.

beats.scene: Romeo and Juliet stand at the window as dawn colours the sky
beats.summary: Romeo spends one night with Juliet and leaves for Mantua at dawn.

beats.scene: Lady Capulet speaks sternly to Juliet while the Nurse stands silent
beats.summary: Juliet's mother tells her she will marry Paris on Thursday.

beats.scene: Lord Capulet shouts angrily in the doorway while Juliet kneels before him
beats.summary: Lord Capulet is furious when Juliet refuses, and threatens to throw her out.

beats.scene: The Nurse speaks quietly to Juliet, who turns her face away
beats.summary: The Nurse tells Juliet to forget Romeo and marry Paris, and Juliet turns to the friar.

beats.scene: Juliet kneels before Friar Laurence, holding a small knife
beats.summary: Juliet begs Friar Laurence for help and says she would rather die than marry Paris.

beats.scene: Friar Laurence holds up a small glass bottle while Juliet listens carefully
beats.summary: Friar Laurence gives Juliet a potion that will make her seem dead for two days.

beats.scene: Juliet holds the little bottle in her hands, alone in her bedroom at night
beats.summary: Juliet pretends to obey her father and then drinks the potion in the night.

beats.scene: The Nurse bends over Juliet in the morning light, shocked and weeping
beats.summary: The Nurse finds Juliet apparently dead on her wedding morning.

beats.scene: Mourners carry Juliet on a flower-covered bier to the family tomb
beats.summary: Juliet is carried to the family tomb as everyone mourns.

beats.scene: Friar John stands at a closed door while guards hold back his path
beats.summary: Friar John cannot leave town because of plague fears, and the letter to Romeo is never delivered.

beats.scene: Balthasar rides up on a tired horse, speaking urgently to Romeo
beats.summary: Romeo's servant Balthasar tells him that Juliet is dead.

beats.scene: Romeo hands over coins to a thin old man in a dusty shop
beats.summary: Romeo buys poison from a poor apothecary in Mantua.

beats.scene: Friar Laurence reads a letter in his cell, his face full of fear
beats.summary: Friar Laurence learns that Romeo never received the letter and hurries to the tomb.

beats.scene: Paris lays flowers at a dark stone tomb under a night sky
beats.summary: At the tomb, Paris lays flowers for Juliet and hides when Romeo arrives.

beats.scene: Romeo and Paris cross swords in the torchlight outside the tomb
beats.summary: Paris thinks Romeo has come to harm the tomb, and they fight; Romeo lays the dying Paris beside Juliet.

beats.scene: Romeo kneels over Juliet in the dim tomb, holding a small bottle
beats.summary: Romeo says goodbye to Juliet, kisses her and drinks the poison.

beats.scene: Friar Laurence stumbles in the dark churchyard, carrying a lantern and a crowbar
beats.summary: Friar Laurence arrives at the tomb too late and finds Romeo dead.

beats.scene: Friar Laurence urges Juliet to leave the tomb, while she looks down at Romeo
beats.summary: The friar tells Juliet that Romeo is dead and begs her to leave.

beats.scene: Juliet lies beside Romeo in the tomb, a small knife in her hand
beats.summary: Juliet ends her own life beside Romeo.

beats.scene: Watchmen with torches enter a graveyard and discover the three bodies
beats.summary: The watchmen find the three bodies, and the Prince and the families are summoned.

beats.scene: The Prince stands with Lord Capulet and Lord Montague before the tomb
beats.summary: The Prince arrives with the two families, and Montague says that his wife has died of grief.

beats.scene: Friar Laurence tells his story to the Prince in front of the grieving families
beats.summary: Friar Laurence explains the whole story of the secret marriage and the potion.

beats.scene: Lord Capulet and Lord Montague shake hands over the bodies of their children
beats.summary: The Capulets and Montagues end their feud at last, and promise golden statues.

beats.scene: The Prince speaks quietly as the grieving families stand together in the morning light
beats.summary: The Prince says that no story was ever more sorrowful than that of Juliet and her Romeo.

The next day, Tybalt asked Romeo to fight, but Romeo said no.
Mercutio was angry, so he fought Tybalt for Romeo.
Mercutio was hurt badly, and he died in the street.

Juliet said sorry to her father, and she drank the potion that night.

B1B2: In the Italian city of Verona, two noble families, the Montagues and the Capulets, have hated each other for years. Nobody remembers why the quarrel began, but it keeps growing, and young people on both sides are drawn into it.
Two Capulet servants walk through the market and see two men from the Montague house. They make rude gestures, and soon the quarrel turns into a fight.
Benvolio, a young Montague, tries to stop the fight, but Tybalt, a fierce Capulet, arrives with his sword drawn. Tybalt hates peace and every Montague, so the fight becomes much bigger.
Prince Escalus, the ruler of Verona, arrives and orders everyone to put down their swords. He is angry and declares that anyone who fights in the streets again will be put to death.
Young Romeo Montague has been wandering alone at night, sighing and crying because he loves a girl named Rosaline. She does not love him back, and his friend Benvolio is worried about him.
A noble young man named Paris asks Lord Capulet for permission to marry his daughter Juliet. Capulet says that she is not yet fourteen, so Paris must wait two more years.
A Capulet servant who cannot read stops Romeo in the street and asks him to read a list of party guests. Romeo discovers that his beloved Rosaline is invited, and he decides to go in secret.
Romeo, Benvolio and their witty friend Mercutio put on masks and walk towards the Capulets' house. Mercutio talks about dreams and a fairy called Queen Mab, but Romeo is too sad to laugh.
At the feast, Romeo catches sight of Juliet and forgets all about Rosaline. He says that he has never truly seen beauty before, and he cannot take his eyes off her.
Tybalt, Juliet's fierce cousin, hears Romeo's voice and knows that a Montague is at the party. He wants to fight, but Lord Capulet orders him to be quiet and respect the feast.
Romeo takes Juliet's hand, and they speak to each other in beautiful words, and then they kiss. Afterwards each of them learns, with horror, that the other belongs to the enemy family.

After the feast Romeo cannot go home, so he climbs the wall into the Capulets' orchard. Juliet appears on her balcony and speaks aloud, not knowing that he is listening, and she wishes that a name meant nothing.
Romeo calls out that he will give up his name if she wishes, and Juliet is startled at first. She warns him that her family will kill him if they find him, but he says that love is stronger.
Juliet says that if his love is true, he must send word tomorrow about marrying her. Reluctantly, they say goodnight over and over as dawn approaches, and he leaves to find the friar.

At dawn, Romeo hurries to Friar Laurence, an old and wise friend who is gathering herbs in his garden. He explains that he has forgotten Rosaline and now loves Juliet, and he wants the friar to marry them.

The friar thinks that Romeo changes his heart very quickly, but in the end he agrees to marry them. He hopes that this strange marriage will finally turn the hatred between the two families into friendship.
Mercutio and Benvolio tease Romeo in the street, and then the Nurse arrives with Juliet's message. Romeo tells her that Juliet should come to the friar's cell that afternoon, ready to be married.

The Nurse complains about her aching bones and teases Juliet for a long time before telling her the news. When Juliet finally hears that she is to be married that afternoon, she runs to the friar's cell.

In the small stone cell, Friar Laurence joins the hands of Romeo and Juliet and marries them in secret. The lovers promise to be faithful to each other for life, and they are happier than they have ever been.
That same day, the hot sun makes everyone short-tempered, and Tybalt finds Romeo and demands a fight. Romeo, who is now Tybalt's cousin by marriage, answers gently and refuses to draw his sword.
Mercutio thinks that Romeo is being a coward, and he draws his own sword to fight Tybalt. Romeo tries to part them, but Tybalt reaches under his arm and wounds Mercutio.
Mercutio laughs at his own wound at first, but then he realises how serious it is. As he dies, he cries out, “A plague on both your houses,” and Romeo is filled with sorrow and anger.
Tybalt returns, and Romeo, blind with grief for Mercutio, draws his sword and fights him. Romeo kills Tybalt, and then realises with horror that he has destroyed his own happiness.
The Prince arrives, and Benvolio tells the true story, but Lady Capulet demands that Romeo should die. The Prince spares him because Tybalt killed Mercutio, but he banishes him from Verona forever.
The Nurse tells Juliet the terrible news, and at first Juliet is angry with Romeo. Then she reminds herself that Tybalt would have killed her husband, and she weeps most for Romeo's banishment.
Romeo hides in the friar's cell, where he lies on the floor, crying that exile is worse than death. The friar scolds him for his weakness and tells him that he is lucky to be alive and married.
Romeo climbs a rope ladder to Juliet's room, where they spend their one night as husband and wife. At dawn they say goodbye, and Juliet is afraid that they may never see each other again.
Lady Capulet comes to Juliet's room and tells her that her father has arranged her marriage to Paris in three days. Juliet is horrified and says that she will not marry him.
Lord Capulet is furious when he hears that his daughter refuses to marry Paris. He shouts that she must go to church on Thursday, or he will throw her out into the street.

The Nurse tells Juliet that Romeo is as good as dead, and that she should marry Paris, who is a much better husband. Juliet is shocked by this advice, and she decides that she can trust no one but the friar.
Juliet hurries to Friar Laurence and begs him to help her, saying that she will kill herself rather than marry Paris. The friar sees that she is in earnest, and he thinks quickly.

The friar gives Juliet a bottle with a sleeping drink that will make her look dead for forty-two hours. He tells her that he will write to Romeo, and that Romeo will be waiting for her in the tomb when she wakes.
Juliet pretends to be sorry and tells her father that she will marry Paris. Lord Capulet is so pleased that he moves the wedding to the next day, and that night Juliet drinks the potion.
On the morning of the wedding, the Nurse comes to wake Juliet and finds her cold and still. Her cries bring Lady Capulet and Lord Capulet, and the house is filled with weeping.
The wedding feast becomes a funeral, and Juliet is carried to the Capulet family tomb with flowers. The whole city of Verona mourns the loss of the young and beautiful girl.

The friar has sent Friar John to Mantua with a letter explaining the plan. But officers suspect that Friar John has been in a house with plague, and they keep him in the town, so the letter never reaches Romeo.
Romeo is in Mantua, happy after a pleasant dream, when his servant Balthasar arrives from Verona. Balthasar brings the terrible news that Juliet has died and is in the Capulet tomb.
Romeo knows of a poor apothecary in Mantua who sells poison, even though it is against the law. The man needs money badly, and in the end, he takes Romeo's gold and gives him the poison.
Friar Laurence hears from Friar John that the letter was never sent, and he fears the worst. He takes a crowbar and runs to the Capulet tomb, where Juliet will soon wake.
That night Paris goes to the churchyard to put flowers on Juliet's grave, and his page whistles a warning when someone comes. Paris hides, and soon Romeo and Balthasar come with tools and a torch.
Paris sees Romeo opening the tomb and thinks he has come to hurt the dead, so the two men fight. Romeo kills Paris, then recognises him and, to grant his last wish, lays him beside Juliet.
Romeo looks at Juliet and thinks that she looks very beautiful, and that death has not yet taken her colour. He kisses her for the last time, drinks the poison and dies beside his wife.
Friar Laurence arrives at the tomb a few minutes too late and finds the dead bodies of Paris and Romeo. At that moment Juliet begins to stir and slowly opens her eyes.

Friar Laurence tells Juliet that Romeo is dead and that they must leave before the watchmen arrive. He begs her to come to a convent, but Juliet will not go, and in his fear the friar leaves her alone.
Juliet finds the empty bottle in Romeo's hand and kisses his lips, hoping that some poison remains. When she finds none, she takes Romeo's dagger, and she dies beside her husband.
The watchmen find Paris, Romeo and Juliet all lying in the tomb. They send for the Prince and the two families, and they arrest Friar Laurence and Balthasar.

The Prince arrives at the tomb with Lord Capulet and Lord Montague, and Montague says that Lady Montague has died of grief because of Romeo's exile. Lord Capulet is crying beside the body of his daughter.

Friar Laurence tells the Prince everything, from the secret marriage to the potion and the letter that was never delivered. He says that he did it all hoping that the families would be friends, and he asks to be punished if he did wrong.
Lord Capulet takes Lord Montague's hand and calls him brother. They promise to build golden statues of Romeo and Juliet, so that Verona will remember the faithful lovers who died.
The Prince tells everyone that a gloomy peace has come with the morning, and that the sun will not shine today. He says that no story has ever been sadder than the story of Juliet and her Romeo.
C1C2: In the sunlit streets of Verona, two noble houses, the Montagues and the Capulets, had been enemies for so long that no one could remember the first insult that had divided them. Their servants quarrelled in the markets, their sons squared up to each other in the squares, and the peace of the whole city was threatened by their rivalry. Out of this bitter soil, however, a very tender love was about to grow.

Two Capulet servants, strolling through the market with their swords hidden under their cloaks, happened upon two Montague men and began to trade insults and rude gestures. The squabble, which began as a joke between hotheads, grew louder and angrier until the swords were drawn and the whole street was in an uproar. Nobody could have said who struck the first blow.

Benvolio, a gentle Montague who loved peace above all things, rushed in with his sword drawn only to separate the fighters, but the fiery Tybalt, a Capulet, took this as a challenge. Tybalt declared that he hated peace as he hated every Montague, and in a moment the brawl spread to dozens of citizens, who ran from the shops with clubs. Verona had not seen such a riot in years.

Prince Escalus, the ruler of Verona, appeared at last and ordered the rioters to throw down their swords in the name of the law. He was furious that the quiet of his city had been broken three times by an old quarrel, and he warned the heads of both houses that the next man to fight in the streets would pay for it with his life. The crowd drifted away in silence.

Romeo, the only son of the Montagues, had taken to wandering alone in the woods before dawn, sighing and weeping over a beautiful girl named Rosaline who had sworn never to love. His parents were anxious about his sadness, and his friend Benvolio, who found the fever of his unreturned affection a little ridiculous, tried to cheer him up. He advised Romeo to look at other girls and forget her.

At the same time, a noble young gentleman named Paris, a relative of the Prince, came to Lord Capulet and asked for the hand of his daughter Juliet in marriage. Capulet, who was fond of his only child, replied that she was not yet fourteen and too young to marry, and he asked Paris to wait two more summers. He invited him to a feast that night, so that he might at least begin to charm the girl.

A Capulet servant, who had been ordered to invite the guests to his master's feast but could not read the list, stopped the first passers-by he saw in the street, who happened to be Romeo and Benvolio. When Romeo discovered that his beloved Rosaline would be at the party, he made up his mind to go in disguise, though Benvolio thought it was a plan of dubious wisdom. They would be wearing masks.

That night, Romeo and his friends Benvolio and Mercutio, all masked, made their way to the Capulets' house, and Mercutio entertained them on the road with a wild speech about Queen Mab, the fairy who visits sleepers and fills their heads with foolish dreams. Romeo, preoccupied with a heavy foreboding that some great misfortune was coming, listened without laughing. Nevertheless, he followed them inside.

Among the torches and musicians of the great hall, Romeo caught sight of a young girl dancing, and at once all thought of Rosaline vanished from his mind. He declared that he had never truly known beauty before that moment and that her brightness taught the torches how to burn. He had to speak to her.

Tybalt, hearing the voice of the masked stranger, knew at once that a Montague had dared to enter the house, and he sent for his sword in a fury. Lord Capulet, however, ordered him to put it away, saying that Romeo behaved like a perfect gentleman and that no blood should be shed at the party. Tybalt was forced to swallow his rage, but he did not forget.

Romeo took Juliet by the hand, and in words as gentle as a prayer, the two strangers spoke of love, and then they kissed. Only afterwards did the Nurse reveal that the girl was a Capulet, while a friend informed Juliet that the boy was the only son of the Montague house, and each of them was struck to the heart. Her love, she said, was born of her only hate.

After the guests had gone, Romeo scaled the orchard wall of the Capulets' house and hid among the trees, and presently Juliet stepped onto her balcony, speaking aloud to the night. She sighed that he was a Montague, and wished that he might change his name, since a rose would smell as sweet by any other name. Romeo, who scarcely dared to breathe, longed to answer her.

Romeo spoke at last, offering to throw away his name if only she would call him her love, and Juliet, startled, asked how he had come to such a dangerous place. She warned him that her kinsmen would murder him if they found him there, but he replied that love had given him wings to climb the wall. Neither of them was afraid.

Juliet, afraid that the whole thing was moving too quickly, told him that if his love was honourable and he meant to marry her, he must send word by a messenger the next day. They said goodnight again and again, each too reluctant to be first to go, until the first grey light of morning began to show in the east. At last Romeo hurried away.

At dawn, Romeo hurried to the cell of Friar Laurence, a wise old friar who was gathering herbs in his garden and was astonished to see the young man awake at such an hour. Romeo explained that he had forgotten Rosaline entirely, that his heart now belonged to Juliet Capulet, and that he begged the holy man to marry them that very day. The old man could hardly believe his ears.

Friar Laurence teased his young friend for the swiftness of his change of heart, but he saw in this surprising love a chance to heal the feud, and in the end he agreed to marry the couple. He hoped that such a marriage might turn the long hatred between the Montagues and the Capulets into lasting friendship, and he blessed the plan with all his heart. Perhaps heaven itself had arranged it.

In the streets, Mercutio and Benvolio teased Romeo for his wild night, and then Juliet's Nurse arrived in search of him, puffing and fanning herself, with a message from her young mistress. Romeo told her in a whisper that Juliet must find some excuse to go to Friar Laurence's cell that afternoon, where she would be made his wife. The Nurse, delighted by the secret, promised to carry the news.

The Nurse sighed and complained of her aching bones and her breathless journey, and she teased Juliet mercilessly by delaying the good news she carried for as long as she dared. When at last she revealed that Juliet was to be married to Romeo that very afternoon, the girl blushed with joy, flew down the stairs and hurried to the friar's cell. Her heart was dancing.

In the cool stone cell, Friar Laurence joined the hands of Romeo and Juliet and, with a short prayer, made them husband and wife in the sight of God, while no other living soul was present. The lovers promised faith and love until death, and they were so intoxicated with their happiness that they could hardly say goodbye. That evening Romeo was to climb to her window with a ladder of rope.

On that hot afternoon, when tempers in Verona ran as high as the temperature, Tybalt found Romeo in the street and called him a villain, hoping to force him into a duel. Romeo, who was now secretly married to Tybalt's cousin, refused to be provoked and told his enemy gently that he loved the name of Capulet more than he could say. Tybalt thought this behaviour merely cowardly.

Mercutio, who could not endure such a disgraceful surrender, drew his own sword and challenged Tybalt in his friend's place, and the two men circled one another in the hot street. Romeo rushed between them, calling out for peace, but Tybalt reached under his arm and gave Mercutio a deep wound, then fled with his companions. All of Verona seemed to hold its breath.

At first Mercutio made a jest of his wound, saying that tomorrow they would find him a grave man, but then he grew weaker and was carried into a nearby house. As he died, he called down a curse on both feuding families, crying, “A plague on both your houses,” and Romeo was overcome by grief that his friend had been hurt in his quarrel. He felt as though his own gentle conduct had caused his friend's death.

When Tybalt returned, still proud and unrepentant, Romeo forgot his gentleness, drew his sword and attacked him, and within a few moments the fierce Capulet lay dead in the street. A cry of terror rose from the crowd, and Romeo, appalled at his own actions, stood as if turned to stone, murmuring that he was fortune's fool. He had destroyed everything in a single minute.

The Prince arrived with the heads of both families, and Benvolio explained exactly what had happened, while Lady Capulet, mad with grief for her nephew, begged for Romeo's death. Since Tybalt had killed Mercutio first, the Prince spared the young man's life, but he banished him from Verona for ever, declaring that if he were ever found there he would die. Mercy, he said, would only murder if it pardoned killers.

The Nurse rushed in wailing, and she was so confused by her own grief that Juliet at first thought that Romeo was dead, and then, when she learned the truth, cursed her husband for killing her cousin. But she soon reproached herself, since Tybalt would surely have killed Romeo, and she wept far more bitterly for the banishment than for her cousin's death. The word “banished” was worse than ten thousand deaths.

Romeo, who had hidden in Friar Laurence's cell, threw himself on the stone floor and wept, crying that exile from Verona was worse than death since it meant exile from Juliet. The friar rebuked him sternly, reminding him that he was alive, that his wife was alive and that the Prince had shown him mercy, and then outlined a plan. Romeo should spend the night with Juliet and leave before dawn for Mantua.

Romeo climbed the rope ladder to Juliet's room, where, for one night, they were husband and wife, and the world and its quarrels were forgotten behind the shutters. At dawn they wept and quarrelled gently about whether the song they heard was a lark, which meant the day, or a nightingale, which meant that it was still night, until it was time to part. Romeo, descending the ladder, promised to write.

Lady Capulet came into the room with news that she thought would please, announcing that Juliet's father had decided that she should be married to Paris on Thursday, in only three days. Juliet, who was already secretly married and desperate to protect her secret, cried out that she would not be the bride of any man, and that she would rather marry Romeo, whom she hated, than Paris. Her mother was astonished.

Lord Capulet, who had expected only gratitude, burst into a rage when he heard that his daughter had refused his choice, and he thundered that she must go to church with Paris on Thursday or never look him in the face again. He swore that if she would not obey, she might starve in the streets for all he cared. Juliet knelt and pleaded, but he would not listen.

Alone with the Nurse, Juliet looked for comfort, but the old woman advised her to forget Romeo, since he was as good as dead, and to marry the handsome Paris, who would make a better husband anyway. Juliet, shocked by the old woman's disloyalty, agreed in a calm voice and then, left alone, resolved that she would never confide in her again. Her only hope now lay with the friar.

Juliet hurried to the friar and found Paris there, politely discussing the wedding, and when he had left, she begged the old man for help, swearing that she would rather die than be the wife of another man. Showing him a small knife, she declared that she was prepared to use it, and the friar, alarmed by the desperation in her face, thought quickly and found a remedy. She had never been more serious.

The friar then produced a small bottle and explained that if Juliet drank its contents on the eve of her wedding, she would fall into a deep sleep that would resemble death for about forty-two hours. She would be laid in the family tomb, he promised, and he would send word to Romeo, who would come to Verona to carry her away when she awoke. The plan was perilous, but it was her only hope.

Juliet returned home and, with downcast eyes, told her father that she was sorry for her disobedience and would marry Paris if he wished, which delighted Lord Capulet so much that he moved the wedding to the next morning. That night, alone in her room and trembling at the thought of waking in the dark among the dead, she drank the contents of the friar's bottle. She fell on the bed like a stone.

On the morning of the wedding, the Nurse went cheerfully to wake the bride, and finding her cold and white in her bed, she screamed with terror and summoned the whole household. Lord and Lady Capulet, Paris and the friar came running, and while the parents cried out in grief, the friar, who knew the truth, quietly urged them to prepare for the funeral. The wedding bells would now ring for the dead.

The wedding feast was turned into a funeral meal, the flowers became a bier, and the joyful music changed to sad bells, as Juliet was borne in solemn procession to the family tomb. All Verona grieved for the daughter of the Capulets, who had died so young and so beautiful, and Paris, who had hoped to be her husband, brought flowers to her grave. Only the friar knew that she was not truly dead.

Friar Laurence had sent a fellow friar, John, to Mantua with a letter that explained everything, but the city officers, suspecting that he had visited a house where illness lay, sealed him inside the building and forbade him to travel. The letter, on which the lovers' whole future hung, was never delivered, and Romeo remained ignorant of the plan. Such small accidents, the friar later said, can ruin great hopes.

In Mantua, Romeo had slept well and woken in good spirits, convinced that a happy dream foretold good news, and was therefore unprepared when his servant Balthasar arrived on a weary horse from Verona. Balthasar, who had seen the burial with his own eyes, told him that Juliet was dead and lay in the Capulet monument, and Romeo, struck dumb, immediately resolved to return. He called for horses and ink.

In despair Romeo remembered a poor apothecary who lived in a tattered shop in Mantua, and he sought him out and offered gold for a poison that would kill swiftly. The man, though he knew that it was forbidden by law to sell it, was so desperate with hunger that he gave way, and Romeo carried the vial away. He meant to die beside his wife.

Friar John returned to Verona and confessed that the letter had been stopped at the gates, and Friar Laurence, who understood at once how dangerous the failure was, took up a crowbar and hurried to the Capulet monument. He knew that Juliet would soon awake and find herself alone among the dead, with no sign of her husband, and he determined to reach her before anything worse should happen. He wrote again to Romeo.

That night Paris, who had loved Juliet in his own gentle way, came to the churchyard to scatter flowers and sweet water on her tomb, and he told his page to whistle if anyone approached. When the sound came, he stepped aside into the shadows, and Romeo appeared with a torch and a crowbar, ordering Balthasar to leave him alone. Balthasar, however, did not go far away and watched from the shadows.

Paris, seeing a Montague breaking into the Capulet tomb, assumed that the man had come to desecrate the dead, and he stepped forward to arrest him in the name of the law. Romeo warned him to go away, since he was in no state to fight, but Paris insisted, and the two men fought briefly until Paris fell. As he died, he asked to be laid beside Juliet, and Romeo, holding up the torch, recognised the man he had killed and granted his dying wish.

Romeo gazed at Juliet, who seemed so beautiful and so fresh that he could not believe that death had really claimed her, and he told her that he would stay with her for ever in that dark house of night. Then, with a last kiss, he drank the poison and lay down at her side. His last thought was of the girl he had loved at first sight.

The friar, stumbling over graves in the darkness with his lantern, arrived at the Capulet tomb only moments too late, and he was horrified to see the bodies of Paris and Romeo lying near the sleeping Juliet. Just then the girl stirred, sighed, opened her eyes and asked where her husband was, and the friar's heart sank. Everything he had planned had gone wrong.

Friar Laurence told her gently that Romeo lay dead beside her, and that a plan beyond all human power had wrecked their scheme, and he begged her to leave the tomb at once before the watchmen came. Hearing voices approaching, he fled in terror, and Juliet, who would not leave Romeo's side, remained kneeling by the one she loved. She would not live without him.

Juliet found the empty bottle in Romeo's hand and kissed his lips, hoping that a little of the poison might remain, but it was all gone, and the lips were cold. Hearing the watchmen's voices coming nearer, she took up his dagger and, with a last whispered word of love, ended her own life, falling upon his breast. She did not wish to wake in a world without him.

The watchmen, seeing the light of their torches fall on the bodies of Paris, Romeo and Juliet, ran to alert the Prince and the families, and they seized Balthasar and the trembling friar. Soon all of Verona was awake, and the citizens rushed through the dark streets crying out the names of the dead. Nobody understood what had happened.

When the Prince arrived with Lord Capulet and Lord Montague, he learned that the Capulets' daughter and the Montagues' son lay dead together, and Montague added in a hollow voice that his wife had died that night of grief for her son's banishment. Capulet, who had come looking for his daughter, wept silently over her body and asked for the hands of his old enemy. They had lost everything together.

Friar Laurence stood before the Prince and explained the whole sad story, telling of the secret wedding, of Tybalt's death and Romeo's exile, of the potion and of the letter that never arrived. He admitted that he had done it all in the hope of reconciling the families, and he offered his own old life as a forfeit if any blame should fall on him. The Prince listened and found no fault.

Lord Capulet reached out his hand to Lord Montague and called him brother, and the two old enemies, after so many years of bitterness, clasped each other at last above the bodies of their children. Montague promised to raise a statue of pure gold to Juliet, and Capulet vowed the same for Romeo, so that the city would remember them for ever. It was a late and terrible peace.

The Prince closed the scene by saying that the morning brought a gloomy peace, and that even the sun, for sorrow, would not show his head, and he ordered everyone to go home and talk of these sad things. He added that some would be punished and some pardoned, for there had never been a story of more woe than that of Juliet and her Romeo. The families walked slowly away, together.
